---
title: "Linearity — Preserve Addition and Scaling"
description: "A compact linear-algebra lesson with mathematical definitions, real values and reasoning."
---

## Start with a question

If you draw two arrows on a tablet and their images appear on a wall, can you predict the image of any combination without testing it?

## Understand the central idea

A linear transformation preserves vector addition AND scalar multiplication. Knowing the outputs of the coordinate basis directions determines the whole transformation.

## Express it with mathematics

$$
T(a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v)=aT(\mathbf u)+bT(\mathbf v)
$$

**Every symbol explained:** T is the transformation; u,v are input vectors; a,b are real-number multipliers. The equation says that combining inputs before transforming equals transforming them separately and combining outputs.

**Substitute real numbers:** If T(1,0)=(2,1) and T(0,1)=(1,−1), then T(3,2)=3×(2,1)+2×(1,−1)=(6,3)+(2,−2)=(8,1).

## Why this works

Every (x,y)=x(1,0)+y(0,1), so preservation of linear combinations forces the output xT(1,0)+yT(0,1). This is why two probes determine a linear map on a 2D input space.

## What can go wrong?

A translation T(x)=x+(1,1) is not linear, because T(0)≠0. The rule also assumes your measured system is actually linear.

## Your turn

Suppose T(1,0)=(0,2) and T(0,1)=(3,0). Compute T(2,−1) without guessing.
